senses.gloss:
indriyanigraha
(‘control of the sense-organs’)
------------------------------------------
All the philosophical systems of India as also the various religions which accept the authority of the Śrutis or the वेदस्, are unanimous that indriya-nigraha or the control of the sense-organs is absolutely necessary to attain मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence.
Mokṣa can be attained either through ज्ञान (knowledge or direct experience of one’s आत्मन्-nature) or through भक्ति (devotion that leads one to God). For either of these paths, मिन्द् is the chief instrument of sādhanā or spiritual practice. Since the इन्द्रियस् or the sense-organs, if allowed to go towards the sense-objects, can make the मिन्द् impure or distracted, there is a great need to reign them in. It is this that is meant by the word इन्द्रियनिग्रह.
Of course, the इन्द्रियस् can and must be directed towards those objects or persons associated with God so that they bring in pure vibrations that help the aspirant to cleanse the मिन्द्.

Indraprastha
------------------------------------------
When the Pāṇḍavas returned to हस्तिनापुर, after their मर्रिअगे with द्रौपदी, धृतराष्ट्र, the blind king, gave them half the kingdom. The Pāṇḍavas desired to build a suitable city for their capital. कृष्ण called विश्वकर्म, the architect of the gods and asked him to build a city at Khāṇḍavaprastha, the level ground, where the Khāṇḍava forest was earlier situated. This had been burnt down by अग्नि the fire-god. अर्जुन and कृष्ण had given him all help and protection in this act.
The city, situated on the bank of the यमुना river, was the most beautiful of all the cities of that time. It was in this city, in their palace of unmatched grandeur, that the Pāṇḍavas conducted the राजसूय sacrifice.
When the Pāṇḍavas decided to leave on their final journey (mahāprasthāna), they crowned the prince वज्र, a grandson of कृष्ण, as the king of इन्द्रप्रस्थ.
The old city of Delhi, it is claimed, is standing at the same site of इन्द्र-prastha.

Indus Valley Civilisation
------------------------------------------
When during the middle of the 19th century the two British engineers who were in charge of constructing a railway-line, got the mounds at हरप्प (now in Pakistan) dug, for getting the burnt bricks to be used as ballast, little did they know that they were digging up a past and hitherto unknown facet of the history of India! It was a great, even exciting, discovery.
Suspecting the existence of the remnants of an ancient civilisation, systematic excavations were undertaken during A. D. 1921-22 by the Archaeological Department of India. These excavations led to the detection of a proto-historic city, now called ‘Harappa’.
Further excavations over the next few decades in about 80 sites, all over India, revealed some more pre-historic cultures and civilisations. However, almost all the cultures cognate to the discoveries at हरप्प, were concentrated in the Sind, Baluchistan and Punjab areas now in Pakistan, a few being found in Gujarat and Rajasthan of India also.
By far, the most extensively researched findings are at हरप्प and मोहेन्जो दारो (both in Pakistan now). The other sites are at Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Lothal, Rangpur (both in Gujarat), Bahawalpur Chānhu Dāro, Amri, Ali Murad, Pandi Wahi, Dabarkot and Quetta (all in Pakistan now).
The archaeological finds at various levels or depths have been assigned to different periods of history, the oldest being 4000 B. C. and the most recent one 2200 B. C.
As regards the nature of this civilisation and culture, whether it was pre-Āryan and pre-Vedic called Draviḍian, several conjectures have been made, mostly by the European scholars. These scholars opine that this civilisation was destroyed by the invading आर्यन्स् around 1500 B. C. However, researches based on the various finds in detail have revealed that this culture of हरप्प and allied sites was a continuation of the Vedic culture, its later phase; and that the आर्यन्स् were indigenous people who had always lived in the Indo-Gangetic plains.
The disappearance of the हरप्प civilisation might have taken place due to the drying up of the सरस्वती रिवेर्, disturbance of the ecological balance and severe climatic changes resulting in a great famine, probably during the period 2200-1900 B. C.
A brief account of the हरप्प and मोहेन्जो दारो civilisation may now be given.
The हरप्प town was a square of about 1.5 kms. (0.9 mile) on each side and about 4.8 kms. (3 miles) in circumference. It was laid out in a grid pattern of streets. The houses were built of burnt bricks whose dimensions conformed strictly to the Kāśyapa Saṁhitā (viz., 11.75" x 5.25" x 7.5" and two more sizes). The houses had only one main door for entrance, fixed in the side lanes. There were courtyards inside, windows opened to the streets. Small houses had just two rooms whereas the bigger ones could have even twenty five rooms. Bathrooms, latrines and sanitary arrangements were very good. Apart from bricks and mortar, wood was generously used, not only for construction purposes but also for a wide range of furniture like cots, chairs, stools, tables and easy-chairs. Firewood and charcoal were in use in the domestic stoves. Rooms were often set apart for purpose of worship.
Language of the Indus ValleyRoads were straight and were maintained well. Special chambers had been constructed for the collection and disposal of garbage.
A clay cart from Mohenjo DaroOne of the most striking features of the हरप्प town was its big granary or warehouse. There were 12 granaries arranged in two parallel rows, with proper arrangements for ventilation and passages of approach. There were also grain millers built on brick platforms where wooden pestles were used for crushing the grains.
Mohenjo Dāro (‘the mound of the dead’) is situated on the west bank of the Indus river, about 600 kms. (375 miles) to the south-west of हरप्प.
This site, better preserved, is larger than हरप्प. The layout is strikingly similar to that of हरप्प.
The chief attraction of this site is what is now called ‘The great Bath.’ It was built of brick set in gypsum mortar with a damp-proof course of bitumen. The dimensions are: 54 by 33 metres (177 by 108 ft.). The outer walls are massive, 2 to 2.5 metres (7 to 8 ft.) in thickness. In the centre there is an open paved quadrangle, with verandahs on four sides. At the back of the verandahs, are galleries and rooms. In the centre of the paved quadrangle is a large swimming bath 11.8 by 7 metres (39 by 23 ft.), which is lined by finely dressed brick laid in gypsum mortar covered with bitumen. There are steps leading down to a low platform for the convenience of the bathers. Arrangements for some kind of steam-bath are also found.
Some features common to all the sites of the इन्दुस् वल्लेय् चिविलिसतिओन् may now be described.
This civilisation was more ancient and comprehensive than the ones of Egypt, Sumeria, Assyria and Mesopotamia.
People were mostly vegetarians and consumed fish also. Apart from wheat, barley and rice, they grew several varieties of fruits and vegetables also like pumpkin, dates and coconuts. They wore clothes made out of cotton, jute and fibres. Several varieties of dressing hair were common among the women. The ornaments used were girdles, ear-rings, bangles, necklaces, nose-rings, anklets, hairpins and beads. Turbans and head-dresses were used by women too.
हरप्प">The Grain Mills at HarappaThe use of metals like gold, silver, lead, tin, copper, nickel, bronze as also many precious stones like diamonds, rubies, emeralds, topazes was well-known to them. Razors for shaving and highly polished mirrors were made out of these metals.
The soldiers used such weapons as bows and arrows, spears, axes, maces, catapults and slings.
Weights and measures had been standardised. One scale discovered in the ruins has very accurate markings.
Trade and commerce by land and by sea were flourishing. Contacts had been well-established with Sumeria, Babylonia and Egypt for trade and commerce.
People were good at arts and crafts also, as can be surmised through the various well-finished toys unearthed from the ruins. Chānhu Dāro town was famous for this.
हरप्प and Mohenjo Daro">Warehouses for grains at हरप्प and Mohenjo DaroMusic and dancing were also known to them. Stringed instruments resembling a vīṇā (lute), cymbals, mṛdaṅga (drum) were in use, as can be guessed through their figures on the seals found.
Pots and jars with various drawings and paintings have been recovered from the site.
Various traditional Indian games like dice-play in current use, were known to them and were in use.
As regards the disposal of the dead, च्रेमतिओन्, बुरिअल् as also leaving the bodies to be eaten up by birds and animals, seem to have existed. Bodies of babies and little children were generally interred in pots and then buried.
A toy cart in clayOne enigmatic aspect of the इन्दुस् वल्लेय् चिविलिसतिओन् is the script discovered on the various seals. All attempts over the last few decades by eminent paleo-graphers to decipher them have not yielded much results. Whether the seals were amulets containing some mantras or whether it is some kind of the earliest form of ब्राह्मी script, it is very difficult to say.
Coming to the religious beliefs, worship of शिव-पशुपति, Goddess दुर्गा, liṅgas and certain animals and trees like bison, fish, serpent, holy basil (tulasī) and peepul tree seem to have existed.
In conclusion it may be said that the इन्दुस् वल्लेय् चिविलिसतिओन् and Culture, represents the later phase of the Ṛgvedic culture and there is no clinching evidence to support the other views that have been hazarded by the European scholars based on insufficient evidence or wrong assumptions.

Indrāṇī
(‘the spouse of इन्द्र’)
------------------------------------------
Most of the deities of the Hindu pantheon have their female counterparts or spouses (called शक्ति). इन्द्र’s शक्ति is इन्द्राणी. Even the Ṛgveda (1.22.12) mentions her as the wife of इन्द्र. In later literature she is known as Śacīdevī. She was the daughter of Puloma, an asura who was the son of कश्यप and दिति.
In iconographical works she is shown with इन्द्र, standing on his left. She holds a blue lotus in her left hand and her right hand is embracing इन्द्र. Her features are beautiful and she is bedecked with many ornaments.
She is sometimes shown as Aindrī, one of the seven mātṛkās (Saptamātṛkās, ‘Seven Little Mothers’). In this form, she may have either six or four hands. The वज्र (thunderbolt) invariably forms one of the things held in the hands, the others being lotus, rosary, water vessel and so on.
Indrāṇī can be worshipped indepen-dently also as the bestower of prosperity. In this aspect, she is shown as seated on a lotus in a pavilion surrounded by the celestial nymphs like ऊर्वशी, Menakā, Rambhā and others.

Indra
(‘one who has great wealth’)
------------------------------------------
Indra, the king of the gods in heaven—hence known as Devarāja or Devendra also—is a familiar figure met with in Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्.
He is undoubtedly the chief deity of the Ṛgveda. Almost a quarter of its hymns, is devoted to praising him. He is the most important deity in the sky. Armed with the thunderbolt (Vajrāyudha) and riding in a chariot whose speed exceeds that of the मिन्द्, he travels everywhere.
His valour is awe-inspiring. His exploits are many. He killed the demon Vṛtra and released the waters imprisoned by him. He clipped the wings of the mighty mountains and made them behave. He recovered the cows of the gods that had been abducted by the demons. He is fond of सोम-drink. Being a war-lord, he became a symbol of the royal power. Hence warriors worshipped him before going to the battlefield.
Indra has often been equated with the Supreme God. His love and affection for his devotees has been eulogized. Scholars opine that इन्द्र may just represent the natural phenomenon of rain being released from the dark clouds as a result of being ‘bombarded by lightning and thunder!’
Indra’s prestige gradually declined and he was relegated to a secondary place by the पुराणस्, retaining however, his place as the king of gods.
In some of the temple sculptures, इन्द्र is depicted in a human form with four arms, riding the celestial elephant ऐरावत.
In the पुराणस् he appears in many roles. For instance:
By his boon कुन्ती conceived and gave birth to अर्जुन, the Pāṇḍava hero.
He sent his chariot and its driver Mātali, to Śrī राम when he began his final battle with रावण.
He killed विश्वरूप, a sage, and thus incurred the sin of ब्रह्महत्या.
By killing Vṛtra, a great devotee of विष्णु, he incurred ब्रह्महत्या once again.
He was deposed by the असुरस् because of the curse of the sage दुर्वासस् whom he had humiliated.
He was cursed by the sage गौतम because of his affair with अहल्या, गौतम’s wife. She was redeemed by Śrī राम later.
Indra is described as a dikpāla, the lord of the eastern direction. He is also associated with rain and thunder.
Actually, इन्द्र is more the title of a ruler in the cosmic scheme, than an individual. Fourteen Indras—like यज्ञ, Rocana, Satyajit and others—have been named in the scriptural works like the Mahābhārata. Purandara, the seventh, is supposed to be ruling in हेअवेन् now.
Any one who successfully performs one hundred अश्वमेध sacrifices in one life, is said to gain the position of इन्द्र.

Indradyumna
(‘One [whose] wealth and power [are like those of] इन्द्र’)
------------------------------------------
One of the oft-quoted incidents from the पुराणस् in support of ārtabhakti (‘devotion of the distressed’) and the immediate response it draws from God is that of Gajendra, the elephant king (vide Bhāgavata 8.2-4).
Gajendra was actually a king, इन्द्र-dyumna by name, in his previous birth. He was the king of Pāṇḍyadeśa. Once he incurred the displeasure of the great sage अगस्त्य and was cursed by him to be born as an elephant.
While roaming in a forest along with his herd, the elephant Gajendra went to a lake to drink water but was caught by a crocodile. After exhausting all his might in his struggle to free himself, he helplessly turned towards Lord विष्णु and prayed piteously. Moved by his prayer, Lord विष्णु arrived on the scene, discharged his famous discus (Sudarśana), killed the crocodile and saved Gajendra’s life.
This story teaches two lessons: The evil effects of dishonouring saints and the power of intense devotion to god.
There is another इन्द्रद्युम्न who was a king of Avantī (or Oṇḍra) and was a great devotee of Lord विष्णु. It was he who established the पुरुषोत्तम क्षेत्र (present पुरी or Jagannāthapurī town), a very holy place of पिल्ग्रिमगे.

indriyas
(‘sense-organs’)
------------------------------------------
The chief instruments with which a human being is equipped, for acquiring knowledge from the external world and react to it, are the इन्द्रियस् or the sense-organs. They are generally grouped into two categories: the ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् (organs of knowledge) and the कर्मेन्द्रियस् (organs of action).
Since they are five in each category, they are also called ‘pañcajñānendriyas’ and ‘pañcakarmendriyas’ (pañca = five).
The five ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् are: śrotra (ear), tvag (skin), चक्षुस् (eye), jihvā or rasanā (tongue) and ghrāṇa (nose).
The five कर्मेन्द्रियस् are: vāk (speech), pāṇi (hands), pāda (feet), pāyu and upastha (organs of evacuation and procreation).
The ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् are produced from the सत्त्व part of the तन्मात्रस् or sūkṣmabhūtas or subtle elements. The कर्मेन्द्रियस् are produced from the रजस् part of the same.
The मिन्द् is also considered as an indriya and is termed as ‘antaḥkaraṇa’ or the inner organ.

Indrajāla
(‘the snare or net of इन्द्र’)
------------------------------------------
Listed among the 64 kalās or sciences and arts, इन्द्रजाल represents the special art of producing illusions, especially in a battle field, to confuse and frighten the enemy. The illusions could be in the form of pictures of their future defeats or the appearance of immense storm-clouds.
Indra, the king of gods, as also some असुरस् (rākṣasas or demons) were experts in this art.
The word ‘indra’ is also interpreted as ‘dexterity’ and not the king of gods.

Indradhvaja
(‘flagpost of इन्द्र’)
------------------------------------------
When the असुरस् (non-gods or demons) were winning the battles against the देवस् (gods) most of the time, the worried gods approached ब्रह्मा, the ड़थेर् of the universe. He took them to विष्णु and apprised him of the problem. विष्णु gave इन्द्र, the king of the gods, a ध्वज or a flag and advised him to fight the असुरस्, keeping this in front. इन्द्र then succeeded in routing the असुरस्. Since then, it became known as ‘Indradhvaja’.
Purāṇas give descriptions of the इन्द्रध्वज and also the method of preparing it with certain kinds of wood as the post.
Kings used to prepare an इन्द्रध्वज and fly it in their kingdoms to please इन्द्र and get rain.
If anyone dreamt that the इन्द्र-ध्वज broke down, it was considered as foreboding evil for the kingdom.
Indradhvaja-पूजा (‘festival of the banner of इन्द्र’) was an ancient festival. As a part of it, perhaps, there was also a sacrifice. The whole festival was a celebration of the victory of the gods, under the leadership of इन्द्र, over the demons.
The festival used to be celebrated in Gujarat at least till the 12th century A. D. It used to be held on Āśvina śukla aṣṭamī (8th day of the bright half of the month of Āśvina—September/October) and continued upto pūrṇimā (full-मोओन् day). Its celebration was believed to ensure a good harvest.

indriyadhāraṇā
(‘restraining the senses’)
------------------------------------------
This is a special term found in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (6.11) though the idea itself is quite common.
The full verse runs as follows: ‘They (the sages) consider that as yoga—the steady control of the senses (sthirām indriyadhāraṇām); the योगि must be vigilant; for योग can be acquired and lost’.
Yoga is perfect concentration of the मिन्द् leading ultimately to the union of the जीव (individual सोउल्) with परमात्मन् (the Supreme सोउल्). This concentration can be attained only when the senses do not function actively, giving rise to mental quietude or tranquillity.
‘Indriyadhāraṇā’ is this holding back of the sense organs and their activity.

Indrajit
(‘One who had conquered इन्द्र’)
------------------------------------------
Indrajit was the most formidable enemy in रावण’s army encountered by राम and लक्ष्मण. He was the son of रावण from his chief queen मण्डोदरी. As soon as he was born he thundered like the rain-clouds. Hence he was given the name ‘Meghanāda’ (‘one who roared like the rain clouds’).
His exploits were many. He once fought with इन्द्र, the king of gods, and defeated him. Thus he got the appellation ‘Indrajit’ (‘one who had conquered इन्द्र’). When हनुमान् was causing a havoc in the अशोक grove after meeting सीता, इन्द्रजित् captured him using the ultimate weapon, the ब्रह्मास्त्र.
In the war with राम’s army, he once made राम and लक्ष्मण swoon with his नागपाश (serpent-weapon). They were later rescued by गरुड (the eagle-mount of विष्णु).
Another magical device he used, to cheat the enemy, was creating a false सीता and beheading her before the enemy’s army. He was finally killed by लक्ष्मण who, with the help of the army of the monkeys, first destroyed the Nikumbhilā sacrifice being performed by him and then used the Aindrāstra.
According to the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (Yuddhakāṇḍa, 9), इन्द्रजित् had obtained a boon from ब्रह्मा that only he who had observed strict celibacy for twelve years could kill him. And, लक्ष्मण had fulfilled this condition.
See also RĀMĀYAṆA.

Indrākṣī
(‘One whose eyes resemble those of इन्द्र’)
------------------------------------------
Indrākṣī is one of the several forms of the देवी (Śakti or पार्वती) often resorted to by the votaries to get rid of diseases like fever, tuberculosis, epilepsy and so on.
According to some works like the Śrītattvanidhi, इन्द्राक्षी has two arms, carrying the वज्र (thunderbolt) in her left hand and showing the gesture of bestowal of boons (varada मुद्रा) in the right hand. Her body is red in colour whereas her garments are yellow. She is well-bedecked with various ornaments. Her face is calm and beautiful. She is surrounded by celestial damsels.
There is a well-known hymn called Indrākṣīstotra attributed to इन्द्र, the king of gods. It is said to be a part of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa. Almost all the names mentioned here are those of पार्वती in her different aspects.
